rationale: B wins because it finds the money story A leaves on the floor: “Nobody has settled on what an AI agent should cost, including Airtable.” A is good, but it buries the same opening as a checklist item — “pricing direction, since pricing is not finalized and a reporter will ask” — which is how a real angle gets demoted into admin homework. Both avoid launch-note mush, but B gives the founder one more structurally distinct route: customer economics, not just product, valuation, and governance.
gaps_in_A: Misses pricing as its own business-model angle. “pricing direction, since pricing is not finalized and a reporter will ask” is treated as proof plumbing when it could be a real SaaS pricing story.
Slightly overstates the business-pressure frame with “pre-AI decacorns rebrand to survive.” The update gives a down-round valuation context and a messaging shift, not evidence of survival pressure.
“formally retiring the ‘spreadsheet-database’ identity” is sharper than the fact block supports. The given fact is a messaging shift, not a formal retirement.
gaps_in_B: “established category leader” and the competitor set “Airtable, Notion, Smartsheet and Monday” are not in the update. Useful market context, but still imported fact.
“Nobody has settled on what an AI agent should cost” is too broad. Airtable’s pricing is unfinalized; that does not prove the whole category is unsettled.
“an unusually candid example” decorates the pricing gap. The facts say pricing is not finalized, not that Airtable is being candid about it.
“bets the company on agents” is punchy but a little hot. The update supports a repositioning, not necessarily an existential company-wide bet.
